title: Maintaining a petrol or diesel generator
subtitle: Oil changes, air filter cleaning, fuel stabiliser, and long-term storage
excerpt: A generator that starts when needed is only reliable if it is maintained on a schedule. Petrol generators need an oil change every 1 to 2 days of use, an air filter clean every 2 days of use, and a fuel stabiliser added if stored for more than 30 days. Diesel generators have a similar schedule with a longer oil-change interval.
sourceNotes: Generator manufacturers' service manuals (Honda EU and GX series, Pramac GSW series) for service intervals and oil specifications. Champion Power Equipment maintenance guide for portable generators. BEAMA generator operation and safety guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A chemical additive mixed into petrol to prevent degradation and gum formation during long storage. Petrol stored without stabiliser degrades in 30 days.

content.text: A petrol generator that sits unused for months accumulates gum in the carburettor from degraded fuel. On the next attempt to start, the carburettor jet is blocked and the engine will not run. This is the single most common failure mode for backup generators. A

attrs.title: Safety: mains electrical
attrs.body: Never connect a generator to the house wiring without a properly installed changeover switch. Back-feeding a generator into the grid can electrocute linesmen working on what they believe is a dead circuit. This is a criminal offence as well as a serious safety hazard.

content.text: Every 25 hours of use (petrol): change the engine oil. Drain hot by running for 2 minutes before shutting down.
Every 2 days of use: clean the air filter element with compressed air or a dry brush. Replace if torn or oil-soaked.
Every 4 days of use or annually (petrol): replace the spark plug. Use the manufacturer-specified plug type and gap.
Monthly (if generator is in use): run for 20 minutes under load to keep the alternator windings dry and the battery charged.
Run the generator for 2 minutes to warm the oil. Shut down and disconnect any load.
Place a drain container under the drain plug. Remove the drain plug with the correct spanner. Allow to drain fully.

Replace the drain plug and tighten to the torque specified in the manual (typically 12 to 15 Nm). Fill with the correct grade: SAE 10W-30 for most small petrol generators below 10°C ambient; SAE 30 for temperatures above 10°C.
Check the oil level with the dipstick. Full level is the upper mark. Do not overfill; excess oil enters the combustion chamber and fouls the plug.
Add fuel stabiliser to the tank and run the engine for 5 minutes to ensure stabilised fuel reaches the carburettor.
Alternatively, drain the tank and carburettor. Run the engine until it stops from lack of fuel.
Store in a dry, ventilated location. Do not store with fuel inside in an attached or internal garage.

rows.symptom: Generator cranks but will not start after storage
rows.cause: Carburettor jet blocked with degraded fuel
rows.fix: Remove and clean the carburettor main jet with carburettor cleaner and compressed air. Replace if the jet is corroded. In future, use fuel stabiliser or drain fuel before storage.

rows.symptom: Generator starts but voltage is low or fluctuating
rows.cause: AVR (automatic voltage regulator) fault, or the brushes in the alternator are worn
rows.fix: Have the alternator inspected by a generator service engineer. This is not a DIY repair.
